Sūrya, desiring brilliance (*tviṣi*), performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). Having sacrificed with it, he obtained brilliance. One who desires brilliance should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.34) A chariot drawn by horses, a bronze armor, and a white horse are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
(ŚŚS 14.34) "May I obtain brilliance through the form of that which possesses brilliance. (ŚŚS 14.34)

In the *nivid*-insertion, there is the mention of Sūrya; that is the form of this day. (ŚŚS 14.34) Varuṇa, desiring rain, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) as rain. Having sacrificed with it, he obtained rain. One who desires rain should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.35) "Upward your eye, O Varuṇa, of beautiful aspect," and "O Indra and Varuṇa, you two for the sacrifice"—in these *nivid*-insertions, there is the mention of Indra and Varuṇa; that is the form of this day. (ŚŚS 14.35)

Bhānumatī, desiring splendor (*tejas*), performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the Āditya. Having sacrificed with it, she obtained splendor. One who desires splendor should sacrifice with it. Regarding the insertion of the *nivid* at the recitation concerning the Āditya [with the verses]: "The sun which is Sūrya," and "And that which is the light of Svarbhānu"—this is the characteristic form (*rūpa*) of this day.

Indra and Viṣṇu, desiring heaven, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) as the means to heaven. Having sacrificed with it, they attained heaven. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.37) In the recitation of the *abhivyāhāra* formulas during the insertion of the *nivid*, that constitutes the characteristic form (*rūpa*) of this day. (ŚŚS 14.37)

The gods and the Asuras contended. Those gods ran to Bṛhaspati as their domestic priest, saying, "Come, learn those two sacrificial rites by which, having sacrificed, we may overcome the Asuras through expulsion. He perceived these two sacrificial rites, Vinutti and Abhibhūti. By means of Vinutti they expelled them, and by means of Abhibhūti they overcame them. In that Vinutti, there are six upward *pṛṣṭhya* stomas and six downward, transverse stomas.

"Having indeed become turned in all directions, they drive away [the enemies]," so it is said. That is the form of the driving away. Now, in the *abhibhūti* sacrifice, there are six *ūrdhva* *pṛṣṭhya-stomas* and six *āvṛtta* *stomas* that are turned toward one another.
"Having become truly upright, they overcome," so it is said.
That is the form of overcoming. Whatever belongs to the Viśvajit with the *bṛhat* as its *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, that is the *śastra* for these two.
The Rāśimarāya [is performed] for one who desires food and drink.
(ŚŚ 14.39) The two final Chandomas are combined.
(ŚŚ 14.39) He gives a thousand cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (ŚŚ 14.39)
For men, [the Soma sacrifice] is later. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) 39.
The common framework consists of the initiation rites (*dīkṣā*) and the *upasad* days. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) 40.
Likewise, the *udayanīyā* [offering]. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) 41.
Two brothers born of successive pregnancies may perform this sacrifice together.
It is the *vighana* [sacrifice] for one who desires to strike away evil and his enemies. At the insertion of the *nivid*, the verses "kayā śubhīyā" and "tad id āsīt" are to be used.

[This is] for one who desires to strike down a rival and one who hates [him]. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases were once in competition. "We shall first go to the heavenly world," said the Ādityas; "We [shall]," said the Aṅgirases. Those Aṅgirases said to the Ādityas, "Tomorrow is our Soma-pressing; do you officiate as priests for us. Agni was their messenger. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)

The Ādityas said: "If these others perform the sacrifice first, they will go to the heavenly world first; the Asuras will then overcome us. We know that sacrificial rite by which we may sacrifice first. They perceived this Sādyaskra sacrificial rite. Having sacrificed with it, they went to the heavenly world as the first. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with it. It has the Trivṛt Stoma.
The Rathantara is the *pṛṣṭha* chant. (3) The recitation (*śastra*) is arranged according to triplets (*ṛc*).
(4) It is an *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice. (5) *ŚŚS* 14.40. (Soma: Other *Ekāhas*)
The altar is the best of barley fields. The northern altar is the threshing floor of barley.
The sacrificial post is the pole of the plow.

The *caṣāla* is made of a bundle of barley stalks. (9) The *vasatīvarī* waters are brought from the family of one who has performed the sacrifice. (10) Curds and honey are carried in leather bags. (11)
Then, with the clarified butter that arises therefrom, they proceed. (Soma:
Other Ekāhas) A horse-chariot is the carrier of the Soma. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) It is used for a distance of one yojana at most. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)
A horse is the sacrificial fee.
(15) On the forenoon, the initiation ceremony (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) takes place. (16) The ritual acts proceed in rapid succession. (17)
The Pravargya rite is omitted.
(18) There are three Upasad days, performed consecutively. (19) The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is dedicated to Agni and Soma. (20)
At the time of the *savanīya* offering, the animal sacrifices share a common ritual procedure (*samāna-tantra*).

(ŚŚS 14.40.21) In place of the barren cow (*vaśā*) dedicated to the Aśvins, which is the *anūbandhyā*, one should sacrifice. (ŚŚS 14.40.22) Or, one should sacrifice with the curd-mixture (*payasyā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. (ŚŚS 14.40.23)
Then they sought after the one who had previously departed. This very [rite] is the rule for the latter;
only the *stomas* are otherwise.
There are eighteen *pavamāna* lauds; the others are threefold (*trivṛt*).
This is that *ukthya* sacrifice brought back [from the *agniṣṭoma*].
It is for the attainment of both desires: that which is in the *agniṣṭoma* and that which is in the *ukthya*.
Go-dhūmā is the urvarā. (6) Go-dhūma is the akhala.
(7) Go-dhūma-kalāpi is the caṣāla. (8) (Soma: Other Ekāhas)
The Vasatīvarī waters are in the Kumbhī jar.
The horse is the carrier of the Soma.
At the end, there is the Traipada rite.
A mare is the sacrificial fee.
This very same is the procedure for the latter [Ekāha],
except that the *stomas* are different.
There are twenty-four *pavamāna* stotras; the others are *trivṛt*.
This is the *vājapeya* brought back [into this form].
It is for the attainment of both that which one desires in the *ṣoḍaśin* and that which one desires in the *vājapeya*.
ŚŚ 14.42. If his hateful rival should sacrifice with the *anukriyā* or the *parikriyā*, or if he should sacrifice with the *parikriyā* or the *utkriyā*.
ŚŚ 14.42. One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with one [set] of three, another set of three, and one [additional] day.
ŚŚ 14.42. For the first [of these], the stotras consist of one [verse] on one day and three [verses] on each of the other two days.
"In three [verses], one [verse] each"—this refers to the subsequent [set].
(ŚŚ 14.42) These consist of twenty-four stotriya verses.
(ŚŚ 14.42) The Gāyatrī meter has twenty-four syllables. (ŚŚ 14.42)
The Gāyatrī [is] splendor and Vedic luster.
(12) By means of these two, one attains splendor and Vedic luster.
(13) The two *śastra* recitations are composed of triplets (*ṛca*). (14)
The Abhijit [is for one] desiring to conquer; (15) the Viśvajit [is for one] desiring to conquer everything. (16) And both of these have three terminuses. (17) (Soma: Other Ekāhas)

Having become Agniṣṭomas, they both established themselves in one another; having become Ukthyas, they established themselves in one another; having become Atirātras, they established themselves in one another.

Indra, desiring to conquer men, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the *Nṛjit*. Having sacrificed with it, he conquered men. Desiring to conquer men, one should sacrifice with it.

Indra, desiring to conquer armies, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the *Pṛtanājit*. Having sacrificed with it, he conquered armies. Desiring to conquer armies, one should sacrifice with it.

Indra, desiring to win the *satrājit* (the all-conquering), performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite, the *Satrājit*. Having sacrificed with it, he won the *satrājit*. Desiring to win the *satrājit*, one should sacrifice with it. From the first three-day period (*tryaha*), the *Nividdhāna* hymns are used during the midday pressings.

Indra, desiring to win wealth, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the Dhanajit. Having sacrificed with it, he won wealth. Desiring to win wealth, one should sacrifice with it. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) It is the twenty-fourth day. (Soma:

Other Ekāhas) Indra, desiring to win the heavenly world, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the Svarjit. Having sacrificed with it, he won the heavenly world. Desiring to win the heavenly world, one should sacrifice with it. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)
This Svarjit sacrifice is like a sacrifice that has fallen into ruin.

(ŚŚ 14.47) Indra, desiring to conquer all, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite, the Sarvajit. Having sacrificed with it, he conquered all. Desiring to conquer all, one should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚ 14.48) The day of the Mahāvrata. (ŚŚ 14.48)

Indra, desiring to conquer all, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) as victorious. Having sacrificed with it, he conquered all. Desiring to conquer all, one should sacrifice with it. (Soma:
Other *Ekāhas*) "Thou hast been born for power, for swift conquest; praise him who is of surpassing might"—this is the insertion (*nivid-dhāna*). (Soma: Other *Ekāhas*)

"From the distant distance you brought forth the embryos from the belly; with boldness you led out him of advancing age"—this is the *udvatī* (verse concerning ascent), which is the characteristic form of this day.

Indra indeed slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ. He delivered the Aruṇmukha Yatis to the jackals. All beings cried out against him. He moved as if sideways away from the gods. Those gods said: "If he continues to move in this manner, the Asuras will overcome us. 1a. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)

"Let us learn that sacrificial rite (*yajña-kratu*) by which we may summon him. They perceived this *Ukthya* sacrifice; with it they summoned him. With that, a king who desires to win over a kingdom should sacrifice. He indeed attains [the kingdom], or he surely falls away. 1b. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) Or he surely falls away.

"O Hero, these invocations of the most frequent singer call upon you as the one to be invoked; you alone are the one to be invoked by the people"—with these words, the *hūtavati* [verse] is placed at the *nivid*. This is the characteristic form of this day.

They cried out against him on account of his being born on a non-sacrificial day (*anaharjāta*), or because of sin, or misfortune. He offered all the pressings (*savana*) to Agni. Agni then consumed all his state of being born on a non-sacrificial day, as well as all his sin and misfortune.

He who is born under an inauspicious constellation, or whom evil speech may address, should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut. For him who knows this and he who sacrifices with it, Agni burns away all ill-fortune arising from being born under an inauspicious constellation and all evil misfortune. (1b) [Soma: Other Ekāhas] One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform it with the *Trivṛt* or the *Triṣṭubh* stoma.
(2) One desiring firm standing (*pratiṣṭhā*) should perform it with the *Catuṣṭoma*. (3)

Everything from the *prātar-anuvāka* (morning recitation) up to the *hāriyojana* cup belongs to Agni. (4) The modification (*ūha*) is according to the purpose. (5) There is a substitution (*pratyāmnāya*) because of a specific scriptural injunction. (6)
"agnim manye pitaram" is the opening verse of the morning recitation (prātar-anuvāka) for the first day.
(ŚŚS 14.51.7) One who desires to obtain the characteristic mark [of Agni] should employ the word "Agni" in the two subsequent rites.
(ŚŚS 14.51.8) Having omitted "pra devatrā," one should recite the fourteen verses beginning with "somasya mā. (ŚŚS 14.51.9)
When the plants are being thrown down, [he recites] "The plants" (RV 10.97).
Having drawn out [the fire], he recites three verses beginning with "Like Aurva and Bhṛgu" (RV 6.15.2–4) and "O mothers" (RV 10.183.1).
Of the verses for kindling the fire by friction, the first and the last are "As they approach" (RV 10.176.1) and "Three hundred" (RV 10.176.2).
"O Agni, enjoy our oblation"—this [verse] is for the *savanīya* offerings at the first, fourth, and fifth [pressings].

(ŚŚS 14.51, 13) "The envoy for you, the all-knowing one"—this is for the offerings to the dual deities. (ŚŚS 14.51, 14) "I praise Agni, the domestic priest"—this is for the cups being drawn. (ŚŚS 14.52, 1)

"agnim dūtam" (RV 1.1.1) is the [first] of the seven *prasthita* offerings. (ŚŚS 14.52, 2) The next four [verses] take the place of the *acchāvāka*sūkta. (ŚŚS 14.52, 3) "agne divaḥ" (RV 8.44.16) is the *yājyā* for the *ājya* offering. (ŚŚS 14.52, 4)
"Upa tvā jāmayaḥ," "agne kaḥ te jāmiḥ," "na yor upabdiḥ," "agnir vṛtrāṇi," "agne sutasya," and "agne dhṛtavratāya"—these are the *tṛcas* for the *prauga* [śastra].
(ŚŚS 14.52) With "agne viśvebhir agnibhiḥ," he performs the *yajyā*. (ŚŚS 14.52) "Kaḥ te jāmiḥ" and "kayā te agne aṅgiraḥ" are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa. (ŚŚS 14.52)
But at the midday [pressing], they are reversed.
(ŚŚ 14.52) "Agni, the slayer of Vṛtras... is for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. (ŚŚ 14.52) "Agni is the head... is for the Acchāvāka. (ŚŚ 14.52)
"Arcantas tvā" is for the Maitrāvaruṇa. (11) "The next [verse]" is for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
(12) "Agnedhṛtavratāya" is the Ṣaḷaha for the Acchāvāka. (13)

They sacrifice with the *uttama* verses. (ŚŚ 14.52) "O Agni, [I praise] you, the god... is [the invitatory verse] for those being lifted up. (ŚŚ 14.53) "Forward to the bright one... is [the offering verse] for the seven *prasthita* offerings. (ŚŚ 14.53)
14.53. [The Śastra] for the Marutvatīya cup is in the northern [part].
3. "O Agni, you are the lord of every people; [you are] of sacrifices"—these are the *pratipad* and the *anucara* of the Marutvatīya. 4.
"O Agni, come hither with the fires" and "Forward your mighty [song]"—these are the two *pragāthas*. 5. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)
"Like fire churned forth, you, O Agni, are the first Aṅgiras, the seer"—these are for the *ekapātinī* verses. "O Agni, may he dwell with us"—this is the insertion point for the *nivid*.
The final verse is the *yājyā*.

"Protect us, O Agni, with one [aid]; protect us, O Agni, from the *rakṣas*": these two *pragāthas* are the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa* for the *niṣkevalya* [śastra]. (ŚŚS 14.54) "Forward to thee, O Agni, the ladle full of oblation": this is the *dhāyyā*. (ŚŚS 14.54) "With this [song] for you, to Agni": this is the *pragātha*. (ŚŚS 14.54)
ŚŚ 14.54: "O Hotṛ" is the Nivid placement.
(Soma: Other Ekāhas) 5. "Agnim naraḥ" is the Yājyā.
(Soma: Other Ekāhas) ŚŚ 14.55: "Agnim agnim vo adhrigum" and "agne jaritar" are the Stotriya and Anurūpa Pragāthas for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) 1.
"Acchā naḥ śīraśociṣam"—this is for the Acchāvāka.
"Agne vivasvat," "tvam agne gṛhapatiḥ," and "tvam it saprathāḥ"—these are the Pragāthas in their proper sequence.
And "yajñasva hotar"—these are the Sūktas.
They sacrifice with the *uttama* verses. (ŚŚ 14.55) "Aganma mahā—" is the *puronuvākyā* for the Āditya cup, and the following verse is the *yājyā*.
(ŚŚ 14.56) "Ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇo adhvarasya hotar" are the nine verses for the cups being filled. (ŚŚ 14.56)
The [offering] of the Hāriyojana cup is in the north. (ŚŚS 14.56) "O Agni, those who seek the Truth..."—these seven verses are for the *prasthita* offerings.
(ŚŚS 14.56) "Forward goes the Hotṛ... is the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) for the Sāvitra cup; the following verse is the offering verse (*yājyā*). (ŚŚS 14.56)
"iyam te navyasī" and "na tvā" are the introductory verse (*pratipad*) and the following verse (*anucara*) for the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra].
(ŚŚ 14.56:6) "tvam agne draviṇodāḥ" and the two following verses—these three are for the *sāvitra* [śastra]. (ŚŚ 14.56:7) The three subsequent verses are for the *ārbhava* [śastra]. (ŚŚ 14.56:8)
There are four [verses] for the *dyāvāpṛthivīya* [śastra]. (14.56.9) Six [verses] from the beginning are for the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra].
(14.56.10) The verse beginning with "abodhi jāraḥ" is for the *vāyavyā* [śastra]. (14.56.11)
"Be pleased with that which is most extensive," [is the verse] for the *surūpakṛtnu* [sacrifice].
(12) "The kindled fire in heaven," [are] three [verses] for the *ekapātinī*s.
(13) "That today of speech," [are] five [verses] for the *janīyā*. (14)
"May he prosper through sacrifice" is the *yājyā* [verse] for [the offering of] ghee;
"They flow toward" is that of the ghee; the following one is that of the *saumya* [offering]. (ŚŚS 14.56–57)
"Ā vo rājānam" is the [stotra] for the Raudra [sastra];
"Vasum na citramahasam" is that of the Māruta;
"Ā no yajñam divispṛśam" and "Ā no vāyo" are the two Pragāthas serving as the Stotriya and Anurūpa for the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.
Or they may be constant.
(ŚŚ 14.57) "O Agni, in the waters... [is the verse] for the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses.
(ŚŚ 14.57) "The gods [placed him] at the foundation... [is the verse] for the *vaiśvadevī* verses. (ŚŚ 14.57)
"Imam ū ṣu vo atithim uṣarbudham"—these four [verses] are for the wives of the gods and for Rākā.
(ŚŚS 14.57.9) "Huve vaḥ sudyotmānam"—these three are of the Akṣarapaṅkti meter. (ŚŚS 14.57.10) "Trimūrdhānam"—these three are for the ancestors (Pitṛs). (ŚŚS 14.57.11)
“*kathā te agne śucayanta āyoḥ*” and the following three [verses] belong to the *yāmī* hymns.
(12) “*mathīd yad īm*” and the following three [verses] belong to the *svāduṣkilīya* hymns.
(13) In the latter two [sections], the [verses] are those of the latter [hymns]. (14)
"Thus Agni with the Gotamas"—this is the concluding verse (paridhānīyā).
(15) When the cups (*graha*) remain unmodified, "Stand, O horses! Praise him!"—these are the *nivid* insertions.
(16) The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is either an ox or gold. (17)
For this is indeed the form of Agni. (18) And having arisen [from that], it is the Agniṣṭoma.
(19) Verily, he who sacrifices with the Agniṣṭut is cut off from all the deities. (20)

Indra, desiring strength, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite, the *Indrastuta*. By sacrificing with it, one obtains strength; therefore, one who desires strength should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.58) When the *nivid* is recited with the mention of Indra, that is the characteristic form (*rūpa*) of this day. (ŚŚS 14.58) Sūrya, desiring splendor, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite, the *Sūryastuta*. By sacrificing with it, one obtains splendor; therefore, one who desires splendor should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.59)
The utterance of "Sūrya" and the placement of the *Nivid* constitute the characteristic form (*rūpa*) of this day.

All the gods (*Viśve Devāḥ*), desiring progeny, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) characterized by the *stotra* for the Viśve Devāḥ. Having sacrificed with it, they procreated. One who desires progeny should sacrifice with it.
The two verses "Imā u tvā purutamasya" and "Vṛṣā mada indra" are used at the placement of the *Nivid*.
"For protection, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra; here Mitra and Varuṇa and Pūṣan"—this recitation for the Viśvedevas constitutes the characteristic form of this day.

Gotama, desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite: the Gotama-rite with four increasing *stomas*. Having sacrificed with it, he attained spiritual luster. One who desires spiritual luster should sacrifice with it.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* [stotra] consists of four [verses].
(Soma: Other Ekāhas) The *ājya* [stotras] consist of eight [verses] each. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) The *mādhyandina-pavamāna* consists of twelve [verses]. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)
In each of the six [days], there are six *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
(ŚŚ 14.61.5) On the twentieth day, there is the Ārbhava-pavamāna. (ŚŚ 14.61.6) The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Caturviṃśa. (ŚŚ 14.61.7)

The *Sāman* is the *antar-ukthya*. (ŚŚS 14.61) The *Pañcaśāradīya*. (ŚŚS 14.62) In the beginning, the Maruts were those who did not share in the drinking of Soma. When the Maruts pressed Soma for Indra, Indra then admitted them to a share in the drinking of Soma. Whoever may be one who does not share in the drinking of Soma, or whoever should desire the same world (*salokatā*) or union (*sāyujya*) with the Maruts, he should sacrifice with this [rite]. (ŚŚS 14.62)
Sixteen oxen, five years old, consecrated for the Maruts, wander about; they are to be immolated as the *savanīya* victims.
(ŚŚS 14.62) The Ṛṣistomas.

(ŚŚS 14.63) Gotama, desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite. Having sacrificed with it, he attained spiritual luster. One who desires spiritual luster should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.63)

Bharadvāja, desiring strength, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). Having sacrificed with it, he obtained strength. One who desires strength should sacrifice with it. Atri, desiring progeny, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite. Having sacrificed with it, he procreated. One who desires progeny should sacrifice with it.

Vasiṣṭha, desiring food, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). Having sacrificed with it, he obtained food. One who desires food should sacrifice with it. Jamadagni, desiring cattle, performed austerities and saw this sacrificial rite. Having sacrificed with it, he obtained cattle. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with it.

Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). Having sacrificed with it, he procreated. One who desires offspring should sacrifice with it. (ŚŚS 14.68) The Pṛṣṭhya days [are performed] in their regular order. (ŚŚS 14.68) The Vrātyastomas [follow]. (ŚŚS 14.69)

ŚŚS 14.69: The Vasus, desiring heaven, performed austerities and saw these sacrificial rites, the Vrātyastomas. Having sacrificed with them, they attained heaven. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with them. ŚŚS 14.70:
[The stomas are] those of Mitra and Varuṇa, the Aśvins, the Vasus, the Maruts, and the Viśve Devas.
ŚŚS 14.70: The Śastra is from the composite Pṛṣṭhya [Stotra].
The *Utkrānti* is an *Atirātra*.

Indra and Viṣṇu, desiring heaven, performed austerities and perceived this sacrificial rite, the *Utkrānti*. Having sacrificed with it, they ascended to the heavenly world. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with it.
The *Nivid* invocations are placed [in the recitation] with the verses beginning "These indeed thee... and "O Indra, he who like the sky...".
"O impetuous one, slay with Viṣṇu as your companion; Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Purandhi"—this [verse] containing the name of Viṣṇu is the characteristic form of this day.

Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin, desiring a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), performed austerities and beheld this sacrificial rite, the tenth day. Having sacrificed with it, he became firmly established. One who desires a firm foundation should sacrifice with it.

The Ṛtustomas. 1. The seasons, desiring heaven, performed austerities and beheld these six sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). Having sacrificed with them, they attained heaven. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with them. 2. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) The Māstomas. 1. The months, desiring the enjoyment of food, performed austerities and beheld these twelve sacrificial rites. Having sacrificed with them, they attained the enjoyment of food. One who desires the enjoyment of food should sacrifice with them. 2. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)
The *ardhamāsa-stomas* (14.77).

The half-months, desiring food, performed austerities and beheld these twenty-four sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). Having sacrificed with them, they obtained food. One who desires food should sacrifice with them. (Soma: Other *ekāhas*) The *nakṣatra-stomas* (14.78). (Soma: Other *ekāhas*)

ŚŚ 14.78. Desiring splendor (*tejas*), the *nakṣatras* performed austerities and beheld these twenty-seven sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*). Having sacrificed with them, they obtained splendor. One who desires splendor should sacrifice with them. ŚŚ 14.79. They are the *ahorātra-stomas*. Desiring food (*annādya*), the *ahorātras* performed austerities and beheld these twenty-seven hundred sacrificial rites. Having sacrificed with them, they obtained food. One who desires food should sacrifice with them.

ŚŚS 14.80. The Muhūrta-stomas. (Soma: Other Ekāhas). Indeed, those desiring food performed austerities and beheld these sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*), numbering ten thousand and eight hundred. Having sacrificed with them, they obtained food. One who desires food should sacrifice with them. ŚŚS 14.81. The Nimeṣa-stomas. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)

ŚŚ 14.81: Those desiring immortality, having performed austerities, beheld these sacrificial rites—ten times ten thousand and eight thousand [verses]. Having sacrificed with them, they attained immortality. One who desires immortality should sacrifice with them. (Soma: Other Ekāhas) ŚŚ 14.82: The Dhvaṃsi-stomas. (Soma: Other Ekāhas)

ŚŚ 14.82. The Dhvamsayas, desiring the infinite, performed austerities and saw these ten and eight times ten thousand sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*). Having sacrificed with them, they attained the infinite. One who desires the infinite should sacrifice with them. ŚŚ 14.83. The Diśām-stomas. The quarters (*diś*), desiring the infinite, performed austerities and saw these four sacrificial rites. Having sacrificed with them, they attained the infinite. One who desires the infinite should sacrifice with them.
The *stomas* of the intermediate directions.

Prajāpati, having created the gods, prepared this food and drink for them—these sacrifices: first the Agniṣṭoma; he did not satisfy them with that. Then the Atyagniṣṭoma; he did not satisfy them with that. Then the Ukthya; he did not satisfy them with that. Then the Ṣoḍaśin; he did not satisfy them with that. Then the Vājapeya; he did not satisfy them with that. Then the Atirātra; he did not satisfy them with that. Then the Āptoryāmaṇa.
The *mahiṣī* cow followed after them.
1. (Soma: Āptoryāman and other *Ekāha*s) It has thirty-three *stotras*. 2. (Soma: Āptoryāman and other *Ekāha*s) It has thirty-three *śastras*. 3. (Soma: Āptoryāman and other *Ekāha*s)
There are thirty-three Ukthya oblations.
Indeed, all the gods are thirty-three. Thus, by means of the stotras, the śastras, and the Ukthya oblations, he gratifies them all individually.
For that [sacrifice], there are nine *stomas* (ŚŚS 15.5.7). There are nine *pṛṣṭhas* (ŚŚS 15.5.8).
There are six *saṃsthās* (ŚŚS 15.5.9).
By way of inclusion, there are twenty-four of them. There are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year;
[this serves] for the attainment of the year itself.
"This sacrifice is indeed 'attained' (āpta), for it encompasses both the gods and the year. Therefore, it is called the *Āptoryāma*.
The *Chandomas* are the *Pavamāna* stotras.
The *Ājya* stotras are the *Trivṛt*, *Pañcadaśa*, *Saptadaśa*, and *Ekaviṃśa* chants.

The *pṛṣṭha* stotras are those with the twenty-seven-fold chant (*triṇava*). (Soma: Āptoryāman and other *ekāhas*) The *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is the thirty-three-fold chant (*trayastrimśa*). (Soma: Āptoryāman and other *ekāhas*) Whatever the *stomas* of the *ājya* stotras are, they are the same for the *atirikta-ukthas*. (Soma: Āptoryāman and other *ekāhas*)

By means of these Agniṣṭoma-stomas on both sides, Prajāpati, having grasped all desires while they were being experienced, deposited them within himself. In the very same way, the sacrificer now, by means of these very Agniṣṭoma-stomas on both sides, having grasped all desires from both sides, deposits them within himself. For the Viśvajit sacrifice with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, the morning pressing is performed with the Hotṛ’s formulas.

In the fourth daily lesson, the *kāyā śubhīya* [is used]; and for the *marutvatīya*, the [stotras] preceding those of the one-day (*aikāhika*) sacrifice are employed. (ŚŚS 15.7) The *pṛṣṭha* chant of the Hotṛ consists of the *Bṛhat* containing the *Vairāja*, or alternatively, the *Rathantara*. (ŚŚS 15.7) The *vāmadevya* containing the *śākvara* is that of the Maitrāvaruṇa. (ŚŚS 15.7)
The Śyaita, containing the Vairūpa as its inner part, or the Naudhasa, belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. (ŚŚS 15.7.4) The Kāleya, containing the Raivata as its inner part, belongs to the Acchāvāka.

But one should first recite the *ātman* [stotra] itself. Or rather, the *anūgarbha* [recitation] follows the *ātman*. Then he settles at the northern sacrificial ground for the gods. There he performs the *saṃsṛp* offerings;
ten offerings over a period of ten nights.

Then [he offers] to Savitṛ the Impeller, to Savitṛ the Inspirer, to Savitṛ the Enlivener, and to Savitṛ of True Impulsion; to Sarasvatī Speech, to Tvaṣṭṛ of Forms, to Pūṣan of Paths, to Indra this one, to Bṛhaspati Splendor, to Soma the King, and to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

"O Savitṛ, the Impeller, I move forward," or "O Savitṛ, the Impeller, I consume [the Soma].
(ŚŚS 15.14.7) Those for whom there are ten generations of Vedic scholars on both sides should perform the sacrifice for him.

Ten [priests] each [drink from] one cup.

When the [sacrifice] with two heifers—one dappled and one spotted, both pregnant—is completed, there follows an offering to Āditya as the first, one to the Viśvedevas, or one to the Maruts as the last.

A ewe for Sarasvatī. (3) A bull for Indra Sutrāman. (4) When the fires have been carried around them, they proceed with the *surā* and the *soma*. (5) (Soma: Rājasūya)
"O Agni, shining with brilliance, purify me with the pure [filter], O God; bestow upon me wisdom and mental powers. With this verse, they worship the flowing Surā. (Soma:
Rājasūya) Or they may worship with verses addressed to the Pitṛs.
(Soma: Rājasūya) "You two [have mixed] the Surāma... is the *puronuvākyā*. (Soma: Rājasūya)
"Let the Hotṛ worship the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra the Good Protector"—this is the *praisha* (direction).
Some authorities prescribe all [the formulas] as modified;
however, one should not do so in that way, for that would be demonic.
"Like a son," is the *yājyā* verse.

(ŚS 15.15) "That which the Aśvins and Sarasvatī squeezed from the Asura Namuci for the sake of power—that bright, honeyed, sparkling King Soma, him I partake of here. This is the *bhakṣa-mantra* for the *surā*.
(ŚS 15.15) "One should purchase a Brāhmaṇa who drinks *surā*"; thus the *bhakṣa* is brought forward. (ŚS 15.15)

an *agniṣṭoma* and an *atirātra*.
Indeed, the dawn breaks for that Brāhmaṇa who recites the Veda.
A Kṣatriya who has attained consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is eligible for this.
Then he performs this sacrifice, the *Kṣatrasya Dhṛti*, by means of an Agniṣṭoma with four stomas and the Rathantara as the *pṛṣṭha* chant. (Śrautasūtra 15.16)
With that *triṣṭoma* sacrifice, Vṛddhadyumna performed the *rājasūya* for Ābhipratārin.

A Brahmin then uttered this prophecy concerning him: "He has not sacrificed with the firmness of a Kṣatriya; the Kurus shall drive him away from Kurukṣetra in battle. And it truly came to pass exactly as he had spoken.
Therefore, one should indeed sacrifice with the Catuṣṭoma.
For the Catuṣṭoma is the foundation of sacrifices;
it is for the sake of firm establishment.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is ten thousand (ayuta).
(16) Indeed, neither from that kingdom nor from that people does one turn away who gives ten thousand.
(17) That is the reason for the name "ten-thousand" (ayuta). (18) (Soma: Rājasūya)
A hundred or even thousands [of sons].

(ŚŚ 15.16.19) Hariścandra, the son of Vidatha and king of the Ikṣvākus, was childless. He had a hundred wives, yet he did not obtain a son through them. Parvata and Nārada were staying in his house; he questioned Nārada. (ŚŚ 15.17.1a) [The Legend of Śunaḥśepa]

"Those who desire this son, both those who know him and those who do not—what indeed does one obtain through a son? Tell us that, O Nārada. Thus questioned with one verse, he replied with ten: "A father pays off his debt in this son and attains immortality, if he beholds the face of his born son while living. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna 15.17)

Whatever enjoyments exist on earth, whatever exist in the fire, and whatever enjoyments exist in the waters for living beings—greater than all those is the enjoyment of a father through his son. (Soma:

The Legend of Śunaḥśepa) Through a son, fathers have forever crossed over the thick darkness; for one’s own self is born from oneself. That [son] is indeed the nourishing and rescuing boat. (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

"What indeed is impurity? What is the deerskin? What are the beard? What is austerity? O Brahmins, desire a son; he indeed is the world that speaks without end. "Food is indeed life; clothing is protection; gold is beauty; cattle are marriages; a friend is a wife; a daughter is indeed a source of pity; but a son is light in the highest heaven."

The husband enters his wife as the embryo; having become the mother, he is born again from her in the tenth month as a new being. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) She is called "wife" (*jāyā*) because [the husband] is born (*jāyate*) again from her. This is the source of manifestation (*ābhūti*); this seed is deposited. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) Both the gods and the seers gathered together that great splendor. The gods said to human beings: "She is your mother once again. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

"This is the broad path, the way of the gods, by which those who possess sons, being free from sorrow, ascend. Even beasts and birds see it; therefore, they engage in sexual union even with their mothers. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) "There is no world for one without a son"—this all beasts know. Therefore, a son mounts his mother and his sister. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

He said: "Tell me how a son may be born to me. He replied to him: "Go to King Varuṇa and say, 'Let a son be born to me; with him I shall sacrifice for you. "So be it," he said. He then approached King Varuṇa. (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

"May a son be born to me; with him I shall sacrifice to you. "So be it," [Varuṇa replied]. A son was indeed born to him, named Rohita. Varuṇa said to him, "A son has been born to you; sacrifice to me with him. He replied: "When an animal is ten days old, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Let him be ten days old, and then I shall sacrifice to you. "So be it. He remained ten days old. Varuṇa said to him: (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

"Or rather, let ten days pass; then perform the sacrifice with this one. He replied, "When the teeth of an animal grow, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Let his teeth grow first; then I shall sacrifice you. (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

"So be it," he replied. His teeth grew back. He said to him, "His teeth have indeed grown back; sacrifice to me with this. He (Śunaḥśepa) said, "When the teeth of an animal grow back again, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Let his teeth grow back again, and then I shall sacrifice to you. (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

"So be it," he said; and indeed, his teeth grew back again. He (the king) said to him: "His teeth have grown back, so sacrifice for me. He replied: "When a Kṣatriya puts on his armor, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; he is not fit for sacrifice until he has put on his armor. Let him first put on his armor, and then I will sacrifice for you. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

"So be it," he replied. He then put on his armor. [Śunaḥśepa] said to him, "You have indeed donned the armor; sacrifice with me. Having said, "So be it," he addressed his son: "This man has indeed given you to me; come, let me sacrifice this man with you. (The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

Saying "No," he took up his bow and retired to the forest. He wandered in the forest for a year. Then Varuṇa seized the King of the Ikṣvākus; his belly swelled. Rohita heard of this, and he went from the forest to the village. Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said to him: (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)
"O Rohita, we have heard that prosperity does not belong to one who is weary from various labors. O Indra among men, the wicked Niṣadha is a companion only to one who wanders.

"Let me wander, Rohita! Let me wander! the Brahmin said to me. Thus he wandered in the forest for a second year. He came from the forest to a village. Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said: [1b] (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

"The fortune (bhaga) of one who sits remains seated; it stands when he stands; it lies down when he lies down; and it moves when he moves. "O Rohita, keep moving! "Keep moving! the Brahmin said to me. So he wandered in the forest for a third year. He came from the forest to a village. Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said to him: [1d] (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa).

"Kali is a man lying down; Dvāpara is he stretching out; Tretā is he standing up; and Kṛta is attained when he is walking. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) "Walk! Walk! Rohita! said the Brāhmaṇa to me. So he wandered in the forest for a fourth year. He came from the forest to a village. Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said: (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

"The two shanks move as if flowering; the self is the one that bears fruit. All his evils lie prostrate, slain by his toil upon the path. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) "‘Roam indeed, Rohita! ‘Roam indeed,’ said the Brāhmaṇa to me. He wandered in the forest for the fifth year. He came from the forest to the village. Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said: (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

"By wandering one finds honey; by wandering one finds the ripe udumbara fruit. Behold the ascetic of the Sun who does not grow weary while wandering. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) "Keep wandering, Rohita! Keep wandering! thus spoke the Brāhmaṇa to me. He wandered in the forest for the sixth year. Then he went from the forest to the village. Indra, approaching him in the form of a man, said: (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

"By wandering one finds honey; by gathering, one finds the *parūṣaka* fruit. By rising up, one finds prosperity; sitting down, one protects nothing at all. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) "O Rohita, keep moving! Keep moving! said the Brāhmaṇa to me. So he wandered in the forest for the seventh year. He came upon the ṛṣi Ajīgarta Sauyavasa in the forest, who, overcome by hunger, was about to eat his own son. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

He had three sons: Śunaḥpuccha, Śunaḥśepa, and Śunolāṅgūla. He said to him, "O Seer, come now; I shall ransom myself with one of these [sons]; I will give you a hundred cows. He, grasping for the eldest, said, "Surely not this one! His mother [said] regarding the youngest, "Certainly not this one! They both agreed upon the middle one, Śunaḥśepa.

Having given him a hundred [cows] and taken him with him, he went from the forest to the village. Having approached his father, he said: "Well then, I shall ransom myself by means of this one. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) Saying "So be it," he addressed King Varuṇa: "I shall sacrifice to you with this one. "So be it," [Varuṇa replied]. "A Brāhmaṇa is indeed superior to a Kṣatriya. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

He taught him this royal consecration sacrifice (*rājasūya*). At that *rājasūya*, he seized a human being as the sacrificial animal. (Śunaḥśepa Legend) Viśvāmitra was his *hotṛ*, Asita was the *udgātṛ*, Jamadagni was the *adhvaryu*, and Vasiṣṭha was the *brahmán*. When the victim had been brought forward, they could not find anyone to bind it. Then Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said: (Śunaḥśepa Legend)

"Give me another hundred, and I will employ him," he said. They gave him another hundred, and he employed him. When he had been brought forward, employed, and the fire had been carried around him, they could not find anyone to serve as the *viśas-tara* (the one who slaughters). Then Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said, "Give me another hundred, and I will slaughter him. They gave him another hundred. He went forth, having unsheathed his sword. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)
Then Śunaḥśepa reflected: "They will surely enter me as if I were non-human; come now, I shall take refuge with the deities. (Śoma:

The Legend of Śunaḥśepa) He first approached Prajāpati among the deities with this Ṛgvedic verse: "To whom now? To which of the immortals? Prajāpati said to him: "You are indeed closest to Agni; go to him for refuge. (Śoma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

He approached Agni with this *ṛc*: "Of Agni, the first of the immortals... Agni said to him, "Savitṛ indeed rules over instigations; go to him alone. He approached Savitṛ with this triplet: "O God Savitṛ, toward you... (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna).

Savitar said to him: "You have been assigned to King Varuṇa; go to him for refuge. Savitar said: "You have been assigned to King Varuṇa; go to him for refuge. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) He approached King Varuṇa with the following thirty-one verses. Varuṇa said to him: "Agni is indeed the mouth of the gods and their heart; praise him, and then I shall release you. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)
He praised Agni with the twenty-two verses that follow this. Agni said to him: "Praise all the gods; then I shall release you. (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

He praised the Viśvedevas with this verse: "Homage to the great ones, homage to the small ones. All the gods said to him: "Praise Indra now, and then we shall release you. He praised Indra with the hymn beginning "Whatever, O true Soma-drinker," and with fifteen verses from the following [hymn]. (Soma: The Narrative of Śunaḥśepa)

Indra, being praised by him, gave him a golden chariot without asking for anything in return. He approached Indra with this verse beginning, "Ever, O Indra... Indra said to him, "Praise the Aśvins now, and then I shall release you. He praised the Aśvins with the next triplet of verses. The Aśvins said to him, "Praise the Dawn now, and then we two shall release you. He praised the Dawn with the very next triplet of verses.

As each ṛc was recited for him, the fetter was further loosened, and the belly of the Ikṣvāku prince became smaller. When the final ṛc was recited, the fetter was completely released, and the Ikṣvāku prince became free from disease. Then the officiating priests said to him: "You alone must bring this day to its conclusion. (The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

Then Śunaḥśepa beheld this *anjas-sava* sacrifice. With the four verses beginning, "Whatever [Soma] you have pressed house by house," he pressed it; and with the verse, "Bring the dregs into the cups," he poured it into the wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*).
Then, while [the sacrificer] held on to him, he offered oblations for him with the first four verses of that very hymn.

Then he led him down to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with these two verses: "O Agni, you are our nearest... and "O Agni, you who know [the way] of Varuṇa... Then he caused him to stand near the fire with this verse: "The tail of Śunaḥśepa, bound by a thousand... (Śoma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa).
Then Śunaḥśepa ran into the lap of Viśvāmitra. Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said to him, "Give me back my son. Viśvāmitra said, "No; for the gods have bestowed him upon me. (Soma:
The Narrative of Śunaḥśepa) He became known as Devārāta Vaiśvāmitra. Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said to him, "Let us both call upon him. He replied, "So be it. (Soma: The Narrative of Śunaḥśepa)
"O descendant of Aṅgiras, you are known by birth as Ajīgarta Śrutakavi. O seer, do not depart from the ancestral lineage; come back to me! (ŚB 15.24). Śunaḥśepa replied:
"They saw you with a sword in hand, for you did not desire [me] among the Śūdras. You chose three hundred cows for yourself, O Aṅgiras. (ŚB 15.24)

Ajīgarta Sauyavasi said to him: "Father, this evil deed committed by me truly torments me. I offer it to you; let a hundred cows be returned to me. Śunaḥśepa replied: "He who once commits an evil act might commit another sin thereafter. Do not fall into the conduct of a Śūdra; what you have done cannot be rectified with you."

"‘He said, “He is not to be allied with,” so Viśvāmitra declared. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna 15.24) ‘“O Prince, speak in such a way that you may inform us; speak so that, being an Aṅgirasa, I may enter into the state of being your son,” [said Śunaḥśepa]. To him, Viśvāmitra replied. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna 15.25)"

"May you be the eldest among my sons, and may your progeny be most excellent. You shall receive my divine inheritance; for this reason, I invite you. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna 1b) Śunaḥśepa replied: "O bull of the Bharatas, speak of me with affection for my sake and for my prosperity, so that I may attain the status of your son. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna 1c)
Then Viśvāmitra addressed his sons:
"O Madhucchandas, listen! O Ṛṣabha, Reṇu, Aṣṭaka, and whoever else you brothers may be—stand for this seniority! Thus he spoke. (Soma: The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

He had one hundred and one sons: fifty-five were elder than Madhucchandas and fifty-five were younger. Those who were the elders did not consider it right; he addressed them, saying, "May your offspring consume the end [of their lineage]. (The Legend of Śunaḥśepa)

"These are the Andhras, the Puṇḍras, the Śabaras, and the Mūcīpas. Moving northward, they are full of bandits; the Vaiśvāmitras are the most numerous among the Dasyus," so they say. Now, those who were younger, beginning with Madhucchandas, considered this to be well-said. Madhucchandas sang: "In that which our father has ordained, in that we all stand firm. We place you in front; we follow after you. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)
Then Viśvāmitra, being gratified, praised his sons:

"O sons, you shall indeed be possessed of cattle and rich in progeny, you who, showing me favor, have made me full of heroic sons. May you all be successful, O Gāthins, with heroic sons and divine gifts as your forerunners; this is my true word to you."

"O Kuśikas, here is the hero Devārata; follow him! Come to you, to your inheritance, and to the knowledge which we possess. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna) Then all those sons of Viśvāmitra, the Gāthins, the Sarāta-s, acting together in unison, stood before Devārata for the sake of seniority and preeminence. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

The seer Devārāta studied both lineages of the Ṛgveda; the Gāthins likewise mastered the lineage of the Jahnus and the divine Veda. This very narrative of Śunaḥśepa consists of more than a hundred Ṛgvedic verses and is immeasurable. He indeed recites it for one who has been consecrated. He recites it while seated upon a golden cushion; he receives [the gift] while seated upon a golden cushion.

"Om" is the response for a *ṛc*; "evam" (so it is) and "tathā" (thus) are the responses for a *gāthā*. "Om" indeed belongs to the divine, and "tathā" belongs to the human. By means of both the divine and the human, he completely releases him from all sin. (Śunaḥśepa-ākhyāna)

Therefore, whatever king may be victorious, even if he does not himself perform the sacrifice, he should certainly have this narrative of Śunaḥśepa recited. For in this [narrative], not even the slightest sin remains. A thousand [cows] should be given to the narrator and a hundred to the respondent; these two should sit upon seats. Even those desiring sons have it recited; they indeed obtain sons, they indeed obtain sons. (The Narrative of Śunaḥśepa)

Brahman, the Self-existent, performed austerity. Having performed that austerity, he reflected: "In austerity, indeed, there is no infinity; come, let me offer myself as a sacrifice into all beings. Having offered himself into all beings, he caused all beings to be offered in the universal sacrifice (*sarvamedha*). Thereupon, he attained preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings.

In this very way, when the sacrificer performs the *Sarvamedha*, having offered himself as a sacrifice among all beings, he causes all beings to offer him as a sacrifice in the *Sarvamedha*. Thereby, he indeed attains preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings. The ritual for the *Puruṣamedha* takes place first.

At the Vājapeya sacrifice, the Brahman priest mounts a chariot wheel made of Udumbara wood with the formula: "By the impulse of Savitṛ, the impeller of strength, may I ascend the highest firmament of Bṛhaspati, whose impulse is true.
(1) If the sacrificer is a Kṣatriya, he says: "Of Indra.
(2) If he is a Vaiśya, he says: "Of the Maruts. (3)
Having sat down upon that pierced chariot wheel, without being prompted, he chants the *sāman* three times. (4) Furthermore, he should also mutter [the following] three times:
(5) "O men, the prize has appeared; the prize-winners have come for the prize. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may the coursers win the heavenly realms. (6) Thus [he recites].
He descends with that very same mantra.
(7) For the descent, the modification is "I have descended.
(8) Having consumed the breath-consumption (*prāṇabhakṣa*) of the honey-cup (*madhugraha*) from a golden vessel, he takes hold of the vessel. (9)
"‘This sacrificer ascends to heaven; this sacrificer ascends to the celestial world,’ [he says] as the sacrificer ascends the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
They cause him to ascend by means of bags of salt-earth (*ūṣapuṭa*).
At the *Rājasūya*, the consecrated sacrificer addresses the *brahmán* five times, saying, ‘O *brahmán*!’"
"In every case, he responds, 'Thou art Brahman.
(1) "At the first [cup], 'Thou art Savitṛ, the impeller.
(2) "At the second, 'Thou art Indra, possessing all power. (3)
"On the third [cup], he recites: 'Thou art Varuṇa, lord of dharma.
(5) "On the fourth, he recites: 'Thou art Rudra, the most gracious.
(6) "On the fifth, he recites only: 'Thou art Brahman. (7)
With his mind, he gives him two golden [plates] that have been turned over.
He accepts them with his mind. The officiating priests of the Aśvamedha, holding the reins, bathe the horse at the two heart-pools where the waters flow together.
"By means of this sacrificial horse, may the king, having sacrificed, be victorious over those who do not honor the Brahmins.
(ŚS 16.18) And if they should touch him on the back while he is the sacrificer, he should mutter: "I and you...
(ŚS 16.18). When the middle day has concluded, they construct palaces in the various directions around the Āhavanīya fire. (ŚS 16.18)
They strike them down from above with walls equipped with traps.
(14) The officiating priests offer oblations of all herbs throughout the night.
(15) At the time of the morning recitation (*prātar-anuvāka*), they descend [from the sacrificial ground]. (16)
The attendants mount [the chariot]. They offer oblations until sunrise.

(17) At this point, having purchased an Ātreya for a thousand [pieces of gold], they take him—who is fair-complexioned, tawny-eyed, wrinkled, covered with freckles, a cripple, and bald—and go toward a woman. (18)
Then, having caused him to enter the water, when the water flows into his mouth, the Adhvaryu offers an oblation upon his head with the formula: "To Bhrūṇahatyā, svāhā! (19).
Then they drive him out. (20).
"Those whose evil has been driven out become free from disease," so it is said. (21).
Now, therefore, follow the *ahīna* sacrifices, each increasing by one [day].

(ŚŚS 16.19) That which consists of one type he obtains by means of the one-night sacrifice (*ekarātra*). (ŚŚS 16.19) Now, that which consists of two types he obtains by means of the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*). (ŚŚS 16.20)

Two indeed are the days and nights; two are heaven and earth; these two are the foundations. Whatever is twofold, whether pertaining to the divine or pertaining to the self, all that he obtains by means of this [rite]. (Soma:
Āhīna) The unmanifest collection of days should undertake the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*).
(Soma: Āhīna) There is a cutting off from the beginning. (Soma: Āhīna)
The final day has the nature of an Atirātra.
(5) There is a sacrificial fee on each successive day.
(6) Those who have not been consecrated perform the sacrifice for one who has been consecrated. (7) (Soma: Āhīna)
The *ahīna* sacrifices conclude with the month.

(8) In the case of a reduction in the number of *sutyā* days, they should increase the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*). (9) One should not recite the *mahāvrata* for one who has been initiated for less than a year. (10)

(ŚŚS 16.20.11) The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the principal among the sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*). (ŚŚS 16.20.13) For the sake of ensuring that there is no deficiency at the opening of the sacrifice. (ŚŚS 16.20.14)

The Abhijit and Viśvajit [sacrifices], or the Caturviṃśa, Mahāvrata, Go, and Āyus [sacrifices]. (18) Whatever is of two kinds, that he obtains by means of the Dvirātra.

These three worlds are indeed three lights; the sacrifice consists of three pressings. Whatever is threefold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he attains by means of this [sacrifice].

For one *jagatī* verse consists of two *gāyatrīs*.

This world is *gāyatra*; thus he finds firm support in this world, in a state of stability from which there is no falling away. The three-night sacrifice of Kusurubindu consists of [the stomas] *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*.
On the first day, he gives three hundred [cows], plus thirty-three and five kalās. On the second day it is the same; on the third day it is the same. (ŚŚS 16.22–16.27)

Only a thousandth part of that [cow] remains. (18) One should redeem that [remaining part] with another cow and make it complete. (19) "It should be made whole," they say, "for the sake of the sacrificer's own prosperity. (22) *Śrautasūtra* 16.22.18–22. (Soma: Āhīna sacrifice)
"Of those who are departing, she who stops first should be [the one to perform the rite]," so they say.
This is a form intended to prevent falling away.
"Of those who are concluding [the sacrifice], she who sits down first should be [the one to perform the rite]," so they say. (ŚŚS 16.22–25)
That is the form for procreation. They say that it should be the most excellent; [one should think], "I have made it the most excellent. (ŚŚ 16.22–28)
In the *Sarvavedas-trirātra*, the Brahman priest is one who has performed the *triśukriya* sacrifice and on both sides of whom there are *śrotriya*s for three generations.
(Soma: Āhīna) Whatever is threefold, that he obtains by means of the *Trirātra*. (Soma: Āhīna) Now, whatever is fourfold, that he obtains by means of the *Caturrātra*. (Soma: Āhīna)
There are four kinds of cattle; moreover, they are four-footed. Whatever is fourfold, whether pertaining to the deities or to the self, all that he obtains by means of this [rite].
The first day has the *trivṛt* stoma; the second, the *pañcadaśa*; the third, the *saptadaśa*; and the fourth, the *ekaviṃśa*.
These four *stomas* are indeed distinct sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) with separate powers. Therefore, for one who knows this, four sons of distinct powers are born among his progeny.
This, indeed, is the four-night sacrifice of Jamadagni.
Now follows the Caturvīra sacrifice of Atri. (Soma:

Āhīna) The morning pressing of the first day has the *trivṛt* stoma; the midday pressing has the *pañcadaśa*; the third pressing has the *saptadaśa*. (Soma: Āhīna) The morning pressing of the second day has the *pañcadaśa* stoma; the midday pressing has the *saptadaśa*; the third pressing has the *ekaviṃśa*. (Soma: Āhīna)

The morning pressing of the third day has seventeen [stomas], the midday pressing twenty-one, and the third pressing twenty-seven. (ŚŚS 16.23.11) The morning pressing of the fourth day has twenty-one [stomas], the midday pressing twenty-seven, and the third pressing thirty-three.
(ŚŚS 16.23.12) They proceed, omitting one stoma each day while producing one [new stoma] each day. (ŚŚS 16.23.13)

By means of that, four heroes of diverse prowess are born from his fore-offerings (*prayāja*); for the *stoma* is indeed a hero. (14) His recitation (*śastra*) follows. (15) The *Rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* of the first [day]. (16) (Soma: Āhīna)
The *Sajanīya* is the *Niṣkevalya*. (17) [In the *Āhīna* sacrifice], the *Nivid* for the second [pressing] is placed either in the *Kayāśubhīya* or the *Tadidāsīt* [hymns].
(18) In the third [pressing], when the *Vairūpa* is the *Pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the third pressing is derived from the *Vairāja*. (19) (Soma: Āhīna)
In the fourth [day], with the Vairāja as the *pṛṣṭha* chant, the third pressing is from the Vairūpa. Or it may be the standard *atirātra*. They call that the Vaiśvānara.
The Abhijit is the fourth of the Ābhiplavika [six-day periods].
(23) The Viśvajit is for the others. (24) Or else, the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata [is the fourth]. (25) (Soma: Āhīna)

Whatever is fourfold, that he obtains by means of the *caturrātra* (four-night sacrifice). (ŚŚ 16.23) Now, whatever is fivefold, that [he obtains] by means of the *pañcarātra* (five-night sacrifice). (ŚŚ 16.24) The *paṅkti* meter has five feet, and the sacrifice is indeed of the nature of the *paṅkti*. Therefore, whatever is fivefold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains by means of this [sacrifice]. (ŚŚ 16.24)

The first day consists of the *trivṛt* stoma; the second, the *pañcadaśa*; the third, the *ekaviṃśa*; the fourth, the *saptadaśa*; and the final day is an *atirātra* with four stomas. This [structure] is indeed by way of the form of these [days]. This very [earth] is the form of the *trivṛt*.
This is for the fifteen-fold [stoma]. (Soma: Āhīna) This is for the twenty-one-fold [stoma]. (Soma: Āhīna) This is for the seventeen-fold [stoma]. (Soma: Āhīna)
This [thumb] belongs to the Catuṣṭoma Atirātra.
Since it is the most excellent among the twenty-one-fold stomas, therefore this [thumb] is the most excellent among these [fingers].
Now, because the Catuṣṭoma Atirātra is the final day, therefore this thumb reaches across all the fingers.
Its weapon is [the *śastra*].
(ŚŚS 16.24) The fourth day is the three-day period consisting of the *ābhiplavika* [form].
(ŚŚS 16.24) Of the fifth [day], there are two pressings (*savana*); the third pressing belongs to the sixth *pṛṣṭhya* [period]. (ŚŚS 16.24)
There are five *ābhiplavika* days.
On the fifth day, the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is from the last [day].
*Abhijit* is the fourth of the *ābhiplavika* days.
The Viśvajit belongs to the others. (18) Or the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata [belongs to the others].
(19) Or for both [the sacrificers], the Abhijit is the fourth and the Viśvajit is the fifth. (20) (Soma: Āhīna)
Whatever is fivefold, that he attains by means of the five-night rite. (Soma:
Āhīna) Now, whatever is sixfold, that [he attains] by means of the six-night rite.
There are six seasons and six *stomas*; therefore, whatever is sixfold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he attains through this. (Soma: Āhīna)
The three-day period consists of the Abhijit, the Viśvajit, and the Vaiśvānara, or else the Mahāvrata.
Or else, immediately after the Abhijit comes the Mahāvrata;
the Viśvajit is the sixth day.
The *pṛṣṭhya* or the *abhiplava* [is performed]. (ŚŚS 16.25) Whatever is sixfold, that he obtains by means of the six-night rite.
(ŚŚS 16.25) Now, whatever is sevenfold, that [he obtains] by means of the seven-night rite. (ŚŚS 16.26)

The seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the seven meters (*chandas*), and whatever exists as the sevenfold with respect to the deities and with respect to the self—all that he obtains by means of this. (Soma: Āhīna sacrifice) The three-day period (*tryaha*) consists of the Abhijit, the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata, and the Vaiśvānara. (Soma: Āhīna sacrifice) Now follows the supplementary sections (*pravalha*) of the year-long sacrifice (*saṃvatsara*). (Soma: Āhīna sacrifice)
The Prākṛta Agniṣṭoma, the Caturviṃśa, the Abhijit, the Viṣuvat, the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata, and the Vaiśvānara—
this indeed is the seven-night sacrifice of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis). They call this very sacrifice the Janaka-saptarātra.
The Abhijit [sacrifice] is the seventh of the Ābhiplavika [six-day periods].
(8) The Viśvajit [sacrifice] is for the others. (9) Or [the Mahāvrata day may be] the Vaiśvānara [stotra] or the Mahāvrata [stotra]. (10)
Whatever is sevenfold, that he obtains by means of the seven-night sacrifice. Now, whatever is eightfold, that he obtains by means of the eight-night sacrifice.

There are eight Vasus; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables. Whatever is eightfold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains by means of this [sacrifice].
The Abhijit is the seventh for those following the Ābhiplavika sequence;
the Viśvajit is for the others. And there is either the Vaiśvānara or the Mahāvrata.

Or, for both [the Abhijit and Viśvajit], the Abhijit is the seventh and the Viśvajit is the eighth. (ŚŚ 16.27) By means of the eight-night sacrifice, one attains that which is eightfold. (ŚŚ 16.27) Now, by means of the nine-night sacrifice, one attains that which is ninefold. (ŚŚ 16.28)

The four quarters, the four intermediate directions, the zenith—this is the ninth. The *bṛhatī* consists of nine syllables. Whatever is ninefold, whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*), all that he obtains by this. The six-day [rite] consists of the Abhijit, the Viśvajit, and the Vaiśvānara; or the Mahāvrata follows immediately after the Abhijit; the Viśvajit is the ninth.
The Jyotis, Agniṣṭoma, Gauḥ Ukthya, and Āyus Atirātra—these three they perform; this is called the *Śalalīpiśaṅga*. (Soma:
Āhīna) That which is ninefold, one obtains by means of the nine-night sacrifice. (Soma: Āhīna) Now, that which is tenfold, one obtains by means of the ten-night sacrifice. (Soma: Āhīna)

The *vilāṭ* consists of ten syllables; it is food, the *virāj*. Whatever is tenfold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that one obtains by means of this.

(Soma: Āhīna) The *abhiplava* is one and a half [days], or there are nine *agniṣṭomas*. (Soma: Āhīna) The ten-night rite (*daśarātra*) is a modification of the sacrificial terminus (*saṃsthā*). (Soma: Āhīna)
And [the Vaiśvānara sacrifice].
With this, Jālu Jātūkarṇya, having sacrificed, attained the priesthood of three eminent families: those of the Kāśis, the Videhas, and the Kosalas.

Śvetaketu, reflecting upon his father’s prosperity, reproached him, saying: "O gray-haired man, you have employed yourself thus for the sake of sacrifices, or rather, to be endowed with prosperity and fame."

He said to him: "Do not speak thus to me, my son. The sacrifice as a ritual act (*yajña-kratu*) is already known to me; it is that very thing which you sought to understand through this entire Brahmanical student (*brahma-bandhu*).
(8) It is indeed said that it was exactly so, just as he had told him.
(9) This is the sacrifice for one who desires the office of a domestic priest (*purodhā*). (10)
He who knows this obtains the office of domestic priest.
(Soma: Āhīna) From the Catuṣṭoma collection comes the recitation of the Trikakud;
then follows the Mahātrikakud. (Soma: Āhīna)
The Chandomas and the Trikakuda;
the Agniṣṭut, Indrastut, Vaiśvadevastut, Pṛṣṭhya, and Vaiśvānara;
the Ṣaḍaha, the Abhijit, the Aśvajit, the Mahāvrata, and the Vaiśvānara.
The ordinary Agniṣṭoma is the ninth or eighth, and the Viśvajit is the tenth. (Soma:
Āhīna) Whatever consists of ten parts, that one obtains through the Daśarātra. (Soma:
Āhīna) Now, whatever consists of eleven parts, that [one obtains] through the Ekādaśarātra. (Soma: Āhīna)

The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables; cattle are of the *triṣṭubh* nature. Therefore, whatever is elevenfold—whether pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) or to the self (*adhyātma*)—all that he obtains by means of this [sacrifice].
(Soma: Āhīna) The ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*) has its meters rearranged (*vyūḍhacchandas*).
(Soma: Āhīna) The *viśvajit* is the eleventh [day]. (Soma: Āhīna)
They call it the Pauṇḍarīka. Ten thousand [cows] are the sacrificial fee. Some say there are eleven thousand horses as the eleventh.

The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) has been explained. These [sacrifices] begin with an *agniṣṭoma* and end with an *atirātra*; they are successive *ahīna* sacrifices, each increasing by one [stotra].
He who knows this attains prosperity that is ever-increasing, the *virāj*, and the enjoyment of food—yea, he who knows this, yea, he who knows this.
Now, therefore, concerning the Mahāvrata.
(The Mahāvrata) Two or three days prior [to the ceremony], the Hotṛ priest fells the plank for the swing from a standing Udumbara tree. (The Mahāvrata)
17.1. To the east of the rising sun. (Mahāvrata) 17.1. If it is not found to the east, then [it may be] to the north. (Mahāvrata) 17.1. If [it is not found] to the south. (Mahāvrata)
Or it may be afterwards.
(Mahāvrata) Having cut it at the root, whether standing facing east or north, he should uproot it if it be a small Udumbara tree.
(Mahāvrata) Or even three planks may be joined together. (Mahāvrata)
It is first as long as his arms;
it is one cubit across;
it is well-planed. (Mahāvrata)
The *prājñāta-agra* (the one with the known tip). 13.
(Mahāvrata) He divides that into four parts at the ends. 14. (Mahāvrata) Then they cut off the two forked branches (*viśākhya*) of this *udumbara* tree or another [tree]. 15. (Mahāvrata)
[He should offer] another man [as a victim].
(Mahāvrata 16) And [he should offer] a bamboo pole.
(Mahāvrata 17) If a *udumbara* tree is not available, he should prepare this [offering] from whatever other fruit-bearing tree there may be that has an auspicious name. (Mahāvrata 18)
Then they have two ropes made of muñja grass.
(Mahāvrata) They should be strong. (Mahāvrata) They should be triple-stranded. (Mahāvrata)
17.2. Beyond that, at a distance of two *vyāyāmas*. (Mahāvrata) 17.2.
This much [space] is around the *hotṛ*. (Mahāvrata) 17.2. They prepare a throne-seat made of *udumbara* wood for the *udgātṛ*. (Mahāvrata)

Its legs are a span (prādeśa) in length. (Mahāvrata) Its head-ribs and side-ribs are a cubit (aratni) in length. (Mahāvrata) Having joined them together, they weave it with double-stranded cords of muñja grass, which are moistened and stretched out straight. (Mahāvrata)
Then they prepare this lute with a hundred strings. (Mahāvrata) Its sounding-box is made of Palāśa wood;
its handle is made of Udumbara wood. (Mahāvrata)
Alternatively, the slaughtering post may be made of Udumbara wood and the staff of Palāśa wood. (Mahāvrata) They bind it around with the hide of a fully red bull, with the hair on the outside.
(Mahāvrata) At its base, they pierce the staff through ten times. (Mahāvrata)
Then they stretch out ten ropes each. (Mahāvrata) They tie them separately at the front.
(Mahāvrata) A lute with a hundred strings has a handle of equal length. (Mahāvrata)

A reed branch with leaves, serving as a speaking-vessel, is prepared. Or it may be a naturally bent blade of *śara* grass. The wives prepare water-jars, small jars, pitchers, lute-like instruments made of bamboo joints, and *piccoras*. (Mahāvrata 17.3.10–12)
One should play the *picchilā* with the mouth near [the instrument] (13). By means of playing, one plays the *kāṇḍavīṇā* (14).
That they call the *ghāṭarī* (15). (The Mahāvrata)
If one plays the *ghāṭarī* drum softly, it will be a source of enemies;
it will produce those who hate [the sacrificer]. (Mahāvrata 16–17) The Adhvaryu prepares four drums (*dundubhi*) that are struck together. (Mahāvrata 1–2)

At the eastern door, on both sides of the door-posts at the junction with the exterior of the *sadas*, he erects two supporting posts. (Mahāvrata) At the western door, on both sides of the door-posts at the junction with the interior of the *sadas*, he erects two supporting posts.
(Mahāvrata) If there are six [posts], one is in the southern half of the *sadas* and one is in the northern half. (Mahāvrata)
They prepare a bundle (*kūrca*) of *muñja* and *kuśa* grass for the *adhvaryu*.
Standing upon it, he responds (*pratyāgṛṇāti*).
Then the other initiated ones each prepare a seat (*bṛsī*) so that they are one span (*prādeśa*) above the ground. (Mahāvrata)
ŚŚ 17.4. Now, for those women who are about to go around the Mārjālīya fire-altar, they prepare nine new jars for each of them.
(Mahāvrata) ŚŚ 17.5. Then they prepare this horse-chariot with its protective fender extended. (Mahāvrata) ŚŚ 17.5. And a bow and thirty arrows. (Mahāvrata)
[The sacrificer] [should choose] either a king or one of royal rank who is an archer.
(Mahāvrata 3) If neither a king nor one of royal rank is available who knows this ritual procedure (*dhi*), then someone else who knows it should perform this.
(Mahāvrata 4) To the north of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, they erect two slanted pillars facing east for the sake of a pit. (Mahāvrata 5)
Then they cover that sacrificial mound (*iḍasamvarta*) or the heap of earth (*utkara*) with a hide. (Mahāvrata) One should not pierce through it with a feathered arrow.
(Mahāvrata) Behind the Āgnīdhra shed, outside the sacrificial ground, they dig a pit (*vaṭa*). (Mahāvrata)
They fasten him [the victim] with the hide of this bull to be immolated, with the neck pointing either eastward or northward and the hair facing upward.
(Mahāvrata 17.5.9) At the proper time, they beat the earth-drum with its tail.
(Mahāvrata 17.5.10) Then they prepare a Śūdra and an Ārya, a woman and a man, as well as a eunuch and a bald man. (Mahāvrata 17.6.1)
This ancient practice has fallen into disuse; it should not be performed when this [present] arrangement has been prepared.
(Mahāvrata) When the tenth day has concluded, they clear away the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds.
(Mahāvrata) They also clear away the Āgnīdhra shed and the Patnīśāla. (Mahāvrata)
Then they spread out a thick layer of fresh *kuśa* grass. (Mahāvrata) They set aside several bundles of *kuśa* grass for the morning seats (*bṛsī*).
(Mahāvrata) Then, during the dead of night, they begin the morning litany (*prātar-anuvāka*) for the Mahāvrata rite. (Mahāvrata)
One should recite [the verses] up to one thousand.
(Mahāvrata) Its stoma is the pañcaviṃśa. (Mahāvrata) The rājan is the pṛṣṭha. (Mahāvrata)
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (Mahāvrata) 5. Now, these [stomas] to be recited around it are the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, Saptadaśa, and Ekaviṃśa. (Mahāvrata) 6.
Either the offering to Indra and Agni, or one from the set of eleven [animals], is the Savanīya. (Mahāvrata) 7.
A bull is for Indra and a goat is for Prajāpati; these two are to be sacrificed.
(Mahāvrata) The one for Indra is recited aloud. (Mahāvrata) The one for Prajāpati is recited in a low voice. (Mahāvrata)

When they proceed to the place where the omenta have been offered, they wash this swing (prenkha) mixed with the sacrificial grass outside the altar. Having entered by the path between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), they carry it around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, bring it into the *sadas* through the eastern door, and place it in front of and to the north of the *hotṛ*'s hearth, facing eastward. (Mahāvrata)
In this very manner, whatever [vessel] is outside the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), they bring it back and place it to the north, according to the path of movement during the ritual progression.

(Mahāvrata) The morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of that [rite] should be in the *triṣṭubh* meter; this is the view of Paiṅgya, as recorded in the *Śuṣkabhr̥ṅgārīya*. (Mahāvrata) "Viśo viśo vo 'tithim" is the *ājya* [stotra]. (Mahāvrata)
Having recited twelve half-verses of that [hymn], he recites the twenty-five-verse hymn beginning with "The men with their thoughts [kindle] Agni from the two fire-sticks" (RV 6.9).
This is the prescribed recitation (diṣṭa-śastra). The Praüga-śastra is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
"kuvid aṅga namasā ye vṛdhāsaḥ"—this is for Vāyu and for Indra-Vāyu.
(Mahāvrata) The [cup] for Mitra-Varuṇa is as at the Viṣuvat.
(Mahāvrata) "ka u śravat katamo yajñiyānām"—this is for the Aśvins. (Mahāvrata)
"Kathā mahām avṛdhat kasya hotuḥ"—this is for Indra (the Aindra).
(8) (Mahāvrata) "Uta syā naḥ sarasvatī juṣāṇā"—this is for Sarasvatī (the Sārasvata). (10) (Mahāvrata) It is arranged as a triplet (tṛca). (11) (Mahāvrata)
For that [Mahāvrata], the Śastra is performed in six sections. (Mahāvrata) Alternatively, the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) may be that of a one-day rite (aikāhika).
(Mahāvrata) The morning pressing is prepared [accordingly]. (Mahāvrata)
Now, therefore, follows the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana).
(Mahāvrata) "Ā tvā ratham yathā ūtaye"—this is the introductory verse (pratipad) for the Marutvatīya hymn. (Mahāvrata) "Idam vaso sutam andhaḥ"—this is the following verse (anucara). (Mahāvrata)

This indeed is the constant *ekāha* *ātāna*. (Mahāvrata) Having first recited the *vāsukra* hymn, "O singer, [the soma] is for me with impetuosity," he places the *nivid* in this *traiṣṭubha* verse: "Great Indra, manly, filling the people... (Mahāvrata) He should recite both hymns in five sections each. (Mahāvrata)
Thus, indeed, is the Marutvatīya [śastra]. (The Mahāvrata) Now, therefore, follows the Niṣkevalya.
(The Mahāvrata) When the morning pressing has been completed, one should have two pits for the swing excavated; such is the established rule. (The Mahāvrata)
"Regarding the *marutvatīya* [cup] at the *praśasta* [recitation]: this is the view of Paiṅgya. (Mahāvrata) 4.

Behind his own *dhiṣṇya* hearth, having measured out a space of four finger-breadths for the footprint, he places a plank there with its grain running northward. Having placed two [stones] on both sides at a distance of four finger-breadths, and having drawn two lines outside those two [stones], he should have two pits for the swing dug—the southern one first, then the northern. (Mahāvrata) 5. They throw up the earth [for the pits] either toward the east or toward the north. (Mahāvrata)
Having placed those two [blades] upon the Viśākhā [post], he lays on a bamboo beam with its tip pointing north. (Mahāvrata) 6.
The Hotṛ measures it with his head. (Mahāvrata) 7. If it be short, he measures it with his arms raised upward. (Mahāvrata) 8.

When it has been firmly settled, he sprinkles it so that the two [ends] do not slip apart. (Mahāvrata) Then he winds this plank of the swing with ropes at its four corners so that it does not fall off.
(Mahāvrata) To the north of the southern swing-pillar, they tie the southern rope. (Mahāvrata)

To the south [of the swing], they tie the northern post of the swing to the northern rope. (Mahāvrata 12) Having pressed it together, he throws it so that it remains at a distance of one span above the ground. (Mahāvrata 13) He sprinkles water over it from above so that it does not shake. (Mahāvrata 15)
Having secured it, he leans it against the northern swing-pillar (preṅkha-sthūṇā). (Mahāvrata) 16.
Once the Marutvatīya Śastra has been recited, he should place it in its proper position. (Mahāvrata) 17.
Then the Adhvaryu, having taken the draught for Mahendra... (Mahāvrata) 1.1.

He sits down facing east in front of the *dhiṣṇya* hearth of the Hotṛ. (Mahāvrata) 17.11. The Hotṛ says to him, "O Adhvaryu, come now and rest. 3. (Mahāvrata) He goes out by the northern door, passing to the north of the northern swing-pillar and to the north of the Adhvaryu; having entered the Āgnīdhra shed by the eastern door, he goes around the north of the Āgnīdhrīya *dhiṣṇya*, sits down behind it facing east, bends his right knee, takes a portion from the vessel of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, and offers it as a libation. 4. (Mahāvrata)

"May I, through the life-span of these—the *Gāyatra* which is long-lived, the *Rathantara* which is all-living, the *Bṛhat-sāman* which is the life of all, the *Vāmadevya* which is the life [itself], and the *Yajñāyajñīya* which is exceeding life—be long-lived. May it move for this breath, for progeny, and for the heart's desire; may it drive away all [enemies] and crush them; may there be a hundred autumns for me, svāhā!"—this is the first [offering]. (Mahāvrata) "To the sky, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! To the earth, svāhā!"—these are the three [offerings]. (Mahāvrata)

"To the cow, svāhā! To speech, svāhā! To the Lord of Speech, svāhā!"—these are three further [offerings]. (Mahāvrata) "What is this" (yad idam), "iti," "haitiham"—one should utter these divine [words] together. We sacrifice that which is for us; let it come swiftly. (Mahāvrata) 4a

"O King, we worship Speech; O Lord of Speech, protect me! May he who seeks to harm us be overcome!
